question: Why do nurses collect a microbiological specimen from a patient?

options.A: To measure the exact white blood cell count in the blood
options.B: To clean out infected tissue from an open wound
options.C: To determine the patient's blood type for transfusion
options.D: To identify the specific microorganism causing an infection

explanation: We collect these samples to find out exactly which germ is making the patient sick, so treatment can hit the right target! [learn more](GST114_U5_T1#GST114_U5_T1_h1)

question: Why is getting the right specimen so important for prescribing antibiotics?

options.A: It allows doctors to prescribe targeted therapy rather than guessing
options.B: It prevents nurses from needing to wear sterile gloves
options.C: It ensures the patient receives the strongest drug available immediately
options.D: It lowers the financial cost of hospital room maintenance

explanation: When we know the exact bug, the doctor can give the right drug instead of just guessing. That stops antibiotic resistance and helps the patient heal faster! [learn more](GST114_U5_T1#GST114_U5_T1_h1)

question: When is the best time to collect a microbiological specimen?

options.A: After the full course of antibiotics is finished
options.B: Twelve hours after stopping all medications
options.D: Immediately after the second dose of antibiotics

explanation: Always collect your sample before starting antibiotics! If the drugs are already in the system, they might kill the germs in the test tube and give you a false negative result. [learn more](GST114_U5_T1#GST114_U5_T1_h2)

question: Which action shows proper infection control when collecting a specimen?

options.A: Recapping used needles using both hands to prevent spills
options.B: Using clean gloves and performing hand hygiene before and after
options.C: Wiping the specimen container exterior with bare hands
options.D: Storing open specimen tubes on the patient's bed sheets

explanation: Hand hygiene and gloves protect both you and your patient from spreading germs. Always clean your hands and glove up! [learn more](GST114_U5_T1#GST114_U5_T1_h2)

question: Why should wooden shaft swabs with cotton tips generally be avoided for bacterial cultures?

options.A: They always cause severe allergic reactions in patients
options.B: They can contain natural toxins that kill fragile bacteria
options.C: They are too flexible to reach most infection sites
options.D: They dissolve too quickly in liquid transport media

explanation: Believe it or not, wood and cotton can have natural substances that kill delicate bacteria, ruining your culture before it even reaches the lab. [learn more](GST114_U5_T1#GST114_U5_T1_h3)

question: What is the main job of the transport media in a collection tube?

options.A: To keep microorganisms alive without letting them multiply
options.B: To change the color of the sample for easy identification
options.C: To chemically digest human cells surrounding the bacteria
options.D: To kill all normal flora present on the swab

explanation: Transport media acts like a safe holding zone. It keeps the germs alive for the lab without letting them multiply out of control. [learn more](GST114_U5_T1#GST114_U5_T1_h3)

question: How should a nurse collect a urine sample from a patient with a catheter?

options.A: By disconnecting the catheter tubing from the drainage bag
options.B: From the rubber sampling port using a sterile syringe
options.C: By squeezing urine backward from the tubing into the bladder
options.D: From the bottom valve of the plastic collection bag

explanation: Always use the special needleless sampling port with a sterile syringe. Never take urine from the drainage bag, as those germs have been sitting there and won't give an accurate lab result! [learn more](GST114_U5_T1#GST114_U5_T1_h4)

question: Why do we usually draw blood cultures from two different sites?

options.A: To reduce the pain experienced in one single arm
options.B: To help distinguish true infection from skin contamination
options.C: To speed up the laboratory processing time significantly
options.D: To collect a larger total volume of blood for testing

explanation: Drawing from two spots helps us know if bacteria in the bottle came from the patient's bloodstream or just from the skin during the poke. [learn more](GST114_U5_T1#GST114_U5_T1_h4)

question: When is the best time for a patient to give a sputum sample?

options.A: At any random time during the afternoon shift
options.B: Early in the morning right after waking up
options.C: Immediately after eating a heavy midday meal
options.D: Right before going to sleep at night

explanation: First thing in the morning is golden! Mucus collects in the airways overnight, giving you a rich, concentrated sample from deep in the chest. [learn more](GST114_U5_T1#GST114_U5_T1_h5)

question: Why should you clean a wound surface with sterile saline before taking a swab for culture?

options.A: To dissolve the stitches holding the wound edges together
options.B: To completely sterilize the interior of the wound
options.C: To numb the local pain receptors in the damaged tissue
options.D: To remove surface contaminants and dead skin cells

explanation: Wiping away surface debris ensures you are culturing the actual infection deep down, rather than just the dust and dead cells on top. [learn more](GST114_U5_T1#GST114_U5_T1_h5)

question: When must you label a specimen container?

options.A: At the nurse's station after finishing all room rounds
options.B: Before entering the patient's room to save time
options.C: Immediately at the bedside in front of the patient
options.D: In the laboratory room before the technician opens it

explanation: Always label right there at the bedside! Never wait until you walk away, or samples can easily get mixed up. [learn more](GST114_U5_T1#GST114_U5_T1_h6)

question: What does the lab usually do if the name on a specimen tube doesn't match the request form?

options.A: Fix the typo themselves without informing the ward
options.B: Reject the specimen and request a new collection
options.C: Call the doctor to guess which patient it belongs to
options.D: Process the sample anyway using the bed number

explanation: Labs have zero tolerance for mismatched names because it's a huge safety hazard. They will throw it out and ask for a fresh sample. [learn more](GST114_U5_T1#GST114_U5_T1_h6)

question: Which of these specimens should NOT be put in the refrigerator if transport is delayed?
explanation: CSF contains very delicate germs that the cold can easily kill. These urgent samples need to stay at room temperature! [learn more](GST114_U5_T1#GST114_U5_T1_h7)

question: What is the main danger of leaving a bacterial swab at room temperature for too long before it gets to the lab?

options.A: Fragile bacteria may die and contaminants may overgrow
options.B: The patient's name will fade off the specimen label
options.C: The transport gel will turn into a solid block of ice
options.D: The plastic shaft will melt and ruin the collection tip

explanation: Time is of the essence! If left too long, fast-growing germs take over, masking the real culprit and ruining the test results. [learn more](GST114_U5_T1#GST114_U5_T1_h7)

question: What should you do if your sterile collection swab accidentally touches the patient's bed sheet?

options.A: Wipe it clean with an alcohol swab and use it
options.B: Proceed with the test because sheets are clean
options.C: Discard the contaminated swab and get a new one
options.D: Blow on the tip to remove any invisible dust

explanation: Once a sterile item touches a non-sterile surface like a bed sheet, it's no longer sterile. Toss it and grab a fresh one—patient safety first! [learn more](GST114_U5_T1#GST114_U5_T1_h8)

question: Which of the following is NOT a consequence of poor specimen collection technique?

options.B: Need for painful repeat sample collection
options.C: Immediate cure of the bacterial infection

explanation: Bad collection leads to wrong results and wrong drugs, which makes the infection drag on—it definitely won't cure it! [learn more](GST114_U5_T1#GST114_U5_T1_h8)
